stories.title: A Stranger Named Paul Used His Car to Save Lives on I-5 in Tacoma
stories.summary: When a driver suffered a medical emergency on I-5, Paul didn't just call 911—he used his own car to push the out-of-control vehicle to the shoulder, preventing a deadly pileup. His quick thinking saved lives and his bravery is being celebrated by Washington State Patrol.
stories.extended_summary: A driver on southbound I-5 near Tacoma suddenly lost control due to a medical emergency, their car weaving at highway speed. Most people would back off and call 911—but Paul made a split-second decision. He deliberately drove his own SUV into the erratic vehicle, pushing it against the concrete barrier until it stopped. The photo shows two white SUVs, dust still settling, one pinned against the divider. No one else was hit. Paul's car was damaged, but the barrier held, and the incapacitated driver was saved from a catastrophic multi-car crash. Troopers called it an act of extraordinary courage.

stories.summary: Quest, a one-year-old dog who was once adopted and returned, is still waiting at the Coachella Valley Animal Campus. A volunteer took him out for a day of adventure, where he calmly met peacocks, goats, and other dogs, showing he's ready for a forever home.
stories.extended_summary: Quest met goats, peacocks, and a donkey without flinching—this one-year-old dog is calm, happy, and full of love. But he's been waiting behind kennel doors since April after being returned by his previous adopters. Volunteer Jen Agnew took him out for the day to show the world his true personality. "Dogs like Quest can spend months waiting," she said. "But outside those walls, we get to show you who they really are."

stories.title: Memories of Boyers, Pennsylvania - Book
stories.summary: Three women from Boyers, Pennsylvania wrote a book of town memories and donated the profits—$1,400 each—to the local fire company and Meals on Wheels. The book is a collection of stories and photos from residents.
stories.extended_summary: After attending town reunions, Antonetta Bell, Kathy Tinker, and Millie Weeter spent years collecting memories from neighbors for a book about Boyers. The book became a hit, so they decided to give back: $1,400 went to the Marion Township Volunteer Fire Company, and another $1,400 to Moniteau Meals on Wheels. The book is still for sale, with proceeds continuing to support the community.

stories.title: Missing puppy returns to family thanks to help from community volunteers
stories.summary: A 5-month-old Australian Shepherd named Jasper went missing near Alderson, West Virginia, sparking a multi-state search. After four days, he was found alive but with both front legs broken, and is now recovering thanks to community support and a GoFundMe.
stories.extended_summary: Jasper, a 5-month-old Australian Shepherd, disappeared on July 10, and volunteers searched by drone, foot, and social media across three states. Four days later, he was found in a neighbor's yard—both front legs broken, but still wagging his tail at the sight of his family. He's now at Fairlea Animal Hospital awaiting surgery, with a GoFundMe helping cover costs as the community rallies around his recovery.

stories.summary: In Montana, "Bar Fairies" leave coffee gift cards on cars left overnight at bar parking lots—rewarding people who chose a sober ride home. The grassroots initiative honors Bobby Dewbre, killed by a repeat drunk driver, and promotes safe choices.
stories.extended_summary: Imagine finding a gift card under your windshield wiper at a bar parking lot—that's the work of the Montana Bar Fairies, who reward sober drivers with free coffee. Their mission: turn tragedy into action and inspire safer choices after a night out.

stories.title: More than a dozen couples wed during Portland Pickles game
stories.summary: Sixteen couples got married or renewed vows during a Portland Pickles baseball game, with the team's co-owner officiating. The ceremonies took place between innings, with 2,000 fans cheering them on.
stories.extended_summary: On a warm Saturday night at Walker Stadium, the chalk first-base line became an aisle, and former NFL punter Jon Ryan officiated as 16 couples exchanged vows. Two ceremonies sandwiched the first and second innings, with baseball fans and family members in the stands. "I've never seen people crying at Walker Stadium before," said team president Alan Miller. The weddings were a first for the ballpark, adding a new chapter to the Pickles' famously fun promotions.

stories.title: NC church’s open gym opens hearts for the gospel
stories.summary: Every Sunday night, men gather at Cary First Baptist Church's gym for pickup basketball—but they end up hearing the gospel. In two and a half years, hundreds have surrendered their lives to Christ, and baptisms have become common.
stories.extended_summary: The gym at Cary First Baptist Church fills with the sounds of dribbling and dunks every Sunday, but before tip-off, the gospel is shared. What started as a simple open gym has become a ministry where hundreds of men have found faith, healing from trauma, and freedom from sin. "They think they're coming to play ball," said worship pastor Mark Page, "but they're really coming to meet Jesus." Baptisms are now a regular sight as lives are transformed.

stories.summary: The San Diego Air & Space Museum is opening its basement restoration department to the public for the first time. Visitors can see volunteers hand-building exact replicas of historic aircraft, like the Hughes H-1 Racer.
stories.extended_summary: For years, the museum's basement was off-limits—a workshop where volunteers craft exact replicas of iconic planes like the Bell X-1 and Hughes H-1 Racer. Now, the public can step into this subterranean world and watch as skilled hands build from scratch using only photos and a tape measure. It's a rare behind-the-scenes look at how aviation history is preserved, one rivet at a time.

stories.summary: New York City is expanding special education programs into preschool classrooms, adding 250 seats across 14 districts. Mayor Mamdani says universal childcare must include kids with disabilities, addressing a longstanding gap in services.
stories.extended_summary: For the first time, NYC is bringing K-12 special education models like Nest and Horizon into preschool, investing $67.5 million. stories.title: Project ME helps menstrual equity around the world
stories.summary: Vanderbilt student Reena Ramani founded Project ME to fight menstrual stigma and provide period products worldwide. The nonprofit now operates in six countries, bringing education and supplies to girls who face barriers due to cultural taboos.
stories.extended_summary: Hearing stories from her immigrant community about menstruation being taboo in parts of India, Reena Ramani started Project ME in high school. The organization now delivers period products and education to girls in Zambia, the DRC, and beyond, tackling both access and stigma. Ramani aims to normalize conversations around menstruation globally.

stories.title: Steamboat Ski Resort Uses Snowmaking Guns to Soak Forest
stories.summary: Steamboat Ski Resort used 41 snow guns to soak nearby forest and slow the Fishhook Fire. In 90-degree July heat, the machines turned into a giant sprinkler system, showing how ski gear can fight wildfires.
stories.extended_summary: When the Fishhook Fire threatened Steamboat Ski Resort, the team got creative. They fired up 41 snow guns in July, turning them into sprinklers to wet down vegetation near Tomahawk and Spike trails. The tactic, also used by Idaho's Tamarack Resort during the 2025 Rock Fire, works on simple physics: wet forest doesn't burn easily. The resort's quick thinking helped keep the fire at bay.

stories.title: Taking Out the Trash on Pittsburgh’s Three Rivers
stories.summary: Friends of the Riverfront organizes weekly cleanups along Pittsburgh's three rivers, removing trash from hard-to-reach spots. Led by Kelsey Ripper, the small team keeps 90 miles of shoreline clean year-round.
stories.extended_summary: On a sunny spring day, volunteers board a boat to a trash-choked shore on the Monongahela River. With grabbers and buckets, they collect sports balls, snack bags, and needles washed downstream. The nonprofit has been doing this for decades, also maintaining the Three Rivers Heritage Trail. Executive director Kelsey Ripper, recently named a 40 Under 40 honoree, runs the 'small but mighty' team of 11.

stories.title: The Garden Path
stories.summary: After his father died, Conner Parrish found healing through beekeeping and gardening. He now runs Bloomistry, a regenerative gardening company that creates spaces for others to find peace and connection.
stories.extended_summary: When Conner Parrish was 18, his father's death left him ungrounded. Reconnecting with nature through beekeeping forced him to stay present and calm—or risk getting stung. He started planting flowers for the bees and eventually founded Bloomistry, a company that uses natural methods to improve landscapes and soil health. In his own garden, he grows peonies and tulips as living tributes to his grandmothers.
